scenarios.title: Add an IPv6 workstation to a team link
scenarios.summary: Choose a unique workstation address and verify direct communication.
scenarios.objective: ExistingPC is 2001:db8:44::10/64 on the team link. Configure NewPC with a different ordinary unicast address in the same /64 and keep its interface up. Preserve ExistingPC’s supplied address/prefix. Check that NewPC can reach ExistingPC and receive its reply. No default route is needed.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Choose a unique workstation address and verify direct communication.
guide.action: Read the full assignment, inspect the device cards, then select the named device. Addresses & interfaces and Static routes are two views of the same saved configuration.

guide.title: Configure and investigate
guide.why: Keep the subnet’s first four full groups and /64. NewPC needs its own interface identifier.
guide.action: Select NewPC → Addresses & interfaces. Do not copy the existing workstation’s whole address.

guide.title: Verify the complete path
guide.why: A forward path alone is not enough. The simulated reply needs a working return route.
guide.action: Choose Check configuration. Open Inspect applied forwarding paths for the source, selected hops and reply; retry any failed requirement.

scenarios.explanation: For this /64, the fixed subnet portion is 2001:0db8:0044:0000. A unique ordinary workstation part such as ::20 keeps both peers on the same link and subnet. The connected route resolves the actual neighbor and the peer uses its connected route for the reply. Equivalent expanded text and other allowed unique addresses pass.
hints: Keep the subnet’s first four full groups and /64. NewPC needs its own interface identifier.
Select NewPC → Addresses & interfaces. Do not copy the existing workstation’s whole address.
A blank, malformed, wrong-prefix, duplicate or reserved choice has a different cause. Read the feedback and retry; many different valid addresses pass.
scenarios.simplifications: Small static IPv6 model with documentation/locally assigned ULA addresses and conventional link-local addresses. Manual on-link prefixes are explicit. No ND/DAD/RA packets, SLAAC, DHCPv6, multicast forwarding, ECMP, recursive next hops, full RFC6724 source selection, IOS/Linux command emulation or real network access. Interface choices and routes are edited natively. Ordinary workstation choices in this unit use /64 and exclude known subnet anycast reservations.

ipv6_teaching.prerequisite_note: IPv4 foundations are useful preparation, but this introduction explains the IPv6 notation needed here. No binary calculation or router command setup is required.

concepts.title: Read an IPv6 address
concepts.text: IPv6 addresses contain 128 bits, written as eight groups separated by colons. Each group has up to four hexadecimal digits: 0–9, then a–f for values ten–fifteen. Leading zeros in a group may be omitted. One :: can stand for enough all-zero groups to make eight groups; it may appear only once.

concepts.title: Keep the subnet part
concepts.text: In these /64 examples, the first four full groups identify the subnet and the final four identify the interface. fd71:55:44::20 expands to fd71:0055:0044:0000:0000:0000:0000:0020. Keep the first half and choose a different ordinary workstation part.

concepts.title: Use the workspace
concepts.text: Select NewPC, keep Addresses & interfaces selected, and type the full address/prefix in its field. Check applies all edited fields and tests the current result. Devices on the same link can talk directly; no default route is needed for this assignment. This manual editor includes a connected/on-link prefix by default; router advertisements are not being simulated.

concepts.title: Choose an ordinary unique address
concepts.text: Each interface on this link needs a different address. IPv6 has no broadcast address: do not subtract an IPv4-style broadcast from its range. The all-zero interface identifier and a small reserved subnet-anycast range are not ordinary workstation choices here; the checker explains these cases.

ipv6_teaching.example_description: ExistingPC uses fd71:55:44::10/64. Give NewPC fd71:55:44::20/64. Load example settings fills the practice fields only; Apply and test example uses them. You can also type the address yourself.
ipv6_teaching.try_change: Change NewPC to fd71:55:44::37/64, then apply and test again. ExistingPC must keep its original address.

scenarios.title: Repair an IPv6 workstation’s path
scenarios.summary: Distinguish a wrong local prefix from an unreachable default next hop.
scenarios.objective: Client must remain 2001:db8:10::10/64. Restore its path to Server at 2001:db8:20::20 and to R1’s office address 2001:db8:10::1. Repair Client’s prefix/default route, keep all supplied interface addresses/prefixes on other devices, and verify replies as well as requests.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Distinguish a wrong local prefix from an unreachable default next hop.
guide.action: Read the full assignment, inspect the device cards, then select the named device. Addresses & interfaces and Static routes are two views of the same saved configuration.

guide.title: Configure and investigate
guide.why: Check whether Client’s connected prefix wrongly includes the server’s network. Then inspect its default next hop.
guide.action: Use Addresses & interfaces for Client’s /64, then Static routes for ::/0 through the actual office router on lan.

guide.title: Verify the complete path
guide.why: A forward path alone is not enough. The simulated reply needs a working return route.
guide.action: Choose Check configuration. Open Inspect applied forwarding paths for the source, selected hops and reply; retry any failed requirement.

scenarios.explanation: The /64 keeps only the office subnet local. The server therefore uses the default route. Its next hop must be R1 on the office link; an unassigned fe80::99 cannot resolve. R1 forwards to the server network, and the server’s default route provides the reply. Repairing only one fault is partial work.
hints: Check whether Client’s connected prefix wrongly includes the server’s network. Then inspect its default next hop.
Use Addresses & interfaces for Client’s /64, then Static routes for ::/0 through the actual office router on lan.
A valid global on-link address for the same router can also work. What matters is a reachable neighboring router and correct current paths.

ipv6_teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on the first IPv6 assignment and the earlier idea of a default gateway. Link-local addresses are introduced here; they do not need a global subnet match.

concepts.title: Decide local or remote
concepts.text: The manually connected prefix tells this model which addresses are local. A mistaken /32 can make a remote destination look local, so the workstation searches the wrong link instead of using its router. Keep the supplied address and repair its /64.

concepts.title: Choose a default router
concepts.text: The route ::/0 is the least-specific default: it catches destinations that do not match a more-specific route. Its next hop is the neighboring router, not the remote server. Here fe80::1 is the router’s link-local address on Client’s lan; the outgoing interface scopes that address to this link.

concepts.title: Edit routes natively
concepts.text: Select Client, then Static routes to edit its default row. Keep destination ::/0, set next hop fe80::1, outgoing interface lan and a usable distance such as 1. Check configuration applies address and route edits together. Inspect applied forwarding paths shows why a request or reply failed. Distance is a preference number used between equally specific active routes; lower is preferred. Leave 1 here.

ipv6_teaching.example_description: Repair Client’s prefix to /64 without changing its fd71:55:10::10 address, then use the office router fe80::1 as its default next hop on lan. The remote server is fd71:55:20::20.
ipv6_teaching.try_change: After the example works, change only the default next hop to fe80::88 and test. Restore fe80::1 and retry.

scenarios.title: Put a link-local next hop on the right link
scenarios.summary: Repair a route’s outgoing interface across a router transit link.
scenarios.objective: R1’s route toward 2001:db8:20::/64 uses R2’s link-local next hop fe80::2, but it points at the wrong outgoing interface. Restore Client’s access to R2’s branch address 2001:db8:20::1 and Server at 2001:db8:20::20, including replies. Keep supplied address/prefix settings, including unnumbered transit interfaces; keep R1 forwarding enabled.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Repair a route’s outgoing interface across a router transit link.
guide.action: Read the full assignment, inspect the device cards, then select the named device. Addresses & interfaces and Static routes are two views of the same saved configuration.

guide.title: Configure and investigate
guide.why: Look at the link labels in the topology. R2’s fe80::2 is on transit, not on the office link.
guide.action: Select R1 → Static routes. Pair the neighboring next hop with the interface that actually reaches that neighbor.

guide.title: Verify the complete path
guide.why: A forward path alone is not enough. The simulated reply needs a working return route.
guide.action: Choose Check configuration. Open Inspect applied forwarding paths for the source, selected hops and reply; retry any failed requirement.

scenarios.explanation: A link-local next hop has meaning only on its chosen outgoing link. Moving the route to transit makes R2 the resolved neighbor. R2’s connected branch prefix and office return route complete both directions. A full route or supported equivalent host routes for both required destinations can meet the outcome.
hints: Look at the link labels in the topology. R2’s fe80::2 is on transit, not on the office link.
Select R1 → Static routes. Pair the neighboring next hop with the interface that actually reaches that neighbor.
The server itself is not directly on the transit link. R2 must receive and forward the traffic, with a return path through R1.

ipv6_teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on local versus remote destinations and a default next hop. This assignment adds a router-to-router transit link and explicit scope.

concepts.title: Link-local means this link
concepts.text: A fe80:: address identifies an interface on one link. It is not forwarded to another link, and the same text may be used on different links. A static route with a link-local next hop therefore needs the correct outgoing interface as well as the address.

concepts.title: Forward to a neighbor, not straight to the remote host
concepts.text: The transit link has link-local addresses only in this model. R1 sends the packet to R2’s transit interface; R2 then forwards it onto the branch network. A directly-on-link route would wrongly search the transit link for the remote server.

concepts.title: Keep both directions
concepts.text: R2 already has the office return route. Keep the supplied address settings and forwarding state; repair R1’s route interface and verify both the branch router and server. This models forwarding decisions, not Neighbor Discovery packet exchange.

ipv6_teaching.example_description: On R1, the route to fd71:55:20::/64 uses neighboring R2 at fe80::2. Select Static routes and choose the transit outgoing interface; the office interface is the wrong link.
ipv6_teaching.try_change: Change R1’s outgoing interface back to office and test the failure, then restore transit. Inspect the selected first hop.

scenarios.title: Find the route that overrides a working default
scenarios.summary: Diagnose why one destination fails while another still works.
scenarios.objective: Client can reach Monitor at 2001:db8:30::30 but cannot reach Server at 2001:db8:20::20. Investigate Client’s static routes and restore both request/reply paths without changing supplied interface addresses/prefixes. Remove an unnecessary faulty route or repair it; valid alternate routing outcomes are accepted.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Diagnose why one destination fails while another still works.
guide.action: Read the full assignment, inspect the device cards, then select the named device. Addresses & interfaces and Static routes are two views of the same saved configuration.

guide.title: Configure and investigate
guide.why: Compare both destinations with the route prefixes. A working default does not guarantee it is selected for every destination.
guide.action: The /64 row wins over ::/0 regardless of their distances. Inspect the next hop of the more-specific route.

guide.title: Verify the complete path
guide.why: A forward path alone is not enough. The simulated reply needs a working return route.
guide.action: Choose Check configuration. Open Inspect applied forwarding paths for the source, selected hops and reply; retry any failed requirement.

scenarios.explanation: The server matches the narrow /64, so its higher distance does not make the default win. The unassigned next hop fails neighbor resolution. Removing the unnecessary narrow route lets the default handle both destinations; repairing it also works. Merely changing its distance to another installed value leaves the same mistake.
hints: Compare both destinations with the route prefixes. A working default does not guarantee it is selected for every destination.
The /64 row wins over ::/0 regardless of their distances. Inspect the next hop of the more-specific route.
Repairing the /64 next hop or removing that row can both work. Keep monitoring access as part of your verification.

ipv6_teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on static route fields and next-hop reachability. This lesson introduces longest-prefix selection before distance.

concepts.title: Specific destinations win first
concepts.text: A router or workstation chooses the matching route with the longest prefix. Only equally specific active routes compare distance. A /64 route therefore beats ::/0 even when its distance is 200 and the default’s is 1.

concepts.title: Fix the misleading row
concepts.text: A route can be installed yet fail to reach its next hop. Increasing its distance does not make a shorter prefix win. Remove an unnecessary bad row, or repair its next hop/interface. Confirm the other service still works afterward.

ipv6_teaching.example_description: Client’s ::/0 route through fe80::1 works for the monitor, but a fd71:55:20::/64 row through fe80::99 breaks the server path. Remove that bad row, or repair its next hop.
ipv6_teaching.try_change: Instead of removing the narrow row, keep its /64 and distance 200 but set its next hop to fe80::1. Both required paths should still work.

scenarios.title: Make the backup route work before the outage
scenarios.summary: Repair a floating default and verify normal and failed-link behavior.
scenarios.objective: Client must prefer its primary interface to reach Server at 2001:db8:20::20, switch to backup when primary is unavailable, and retain primary when backup is unavailable. Repair its default routes and preserve all supplied interface addresses/prefixes. Keep the saved base interfaces up. Check runs three separate simulated conditions and verifies replies and the first outgoing interface; equivalent usable distance pairs are accepted.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Repair a floating default and verify normal and failed-link behavior.
guide.action: Read the full assignment, inspect the device cards, then select the named device. Addresses & interfaces and Static routes are two views of the same saved configuration.

guide.title: Configure and investigate
guide.why: Normal reachability alone does not exercise the backup next hop. Read all three condition results.
guide.action: Select Client → Static routes. The backup next hop must resolve on backup, and its route must remain less preferred than primary.

guide.title: Verify the complete path
guide.why: A forward path alone is not enough. The simulated reply needs a working return route.
guide.action: Choose Check configuration. Open Inspect applied forwarding paths for the source, selected hops and reply; retry any failed requirement.

scenarios.explanation: With equally specific defaults, primary wins by lower distance. When primary is down its row is inactive; backup must resolve its own neighboring router and carry both directions. The checker uses clones for failures and checks the actual first hop, so one happy-path ping, reversed preference or a single permanent route does not pass.
hints: Normal reachability alone does not exercise the backup next hop. Read all three condition results.
Select Client → Static routes. The backup next hop must resolve on backup, and its route must remain less preferred than primary.
Different unequal distances can be valid. Reversing preference or disabling a base interface cannot substitute for a working normal-and-failure configuration.

ipv6_teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on longest-prefix and route distance. This lesson adds deterministic failure cases and preference verification.

concepts.title: Prefer one route, retain another
concepts.text: Two equally specific routes can use different distances. The lower distance is preferred while its interface is up. A higher-distance route is a floating backup; it becomes useful when the preferred route is no longer active. This model does not infer link failure from a silent neighbor timeout.

concepts.title: Test the backup before relying on it
concepts.text: Normal success can hide a broken backup. The checker tests the current configuration, then a copy with primary down and another with backup down. The saved base state is not changed. The first interface must match the requested preference in each case.

concepts.title: Keep a usable pair
concepts.text: Use distinct distances, usable next-hop neighbors and the correct outgoing interfaces. Equal-cost choices are explicitly unsupported in this first static model. No particular pair of numeric distances is required if preference and failure behavior are correct.

ipv6_teaching.example_description: Client has two office links. Keep the primary default preferred and repair the backup default’s next hop to fe80::1 on backup. Apply tests normal operation and each single-interface failure using separate simulated copies.
ipv6_teaching.try_change: Use distances 5 for primary and 50 for backup. The same preference and failure checks should pass. Reverse them to see the normal-preference feedback.

scenarios.title: Recover an IPv6 branch handover
scenarios.summary: Combine prefix repair, scoped routing, forwarding and return-path diagnosis.
scenarios.objective: Restore Client’s access to R2’s branch address 2001:db8:20::1 and Server at 2001:db8:20::20, including replies. Client must keep address 2001:db8:10::10 with the correct /64. Keep all other supplied address/prefix settings, including link-local-only transit interfaces. Investigate Client, R1 and Server; repair the source prefix, transit forwarding/next hop and server return route. R1 must forward between its networks.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: Combine prefix repair, scoped routing, forwarding and return-path diagnosis.
guide.action: Read the full assignment, inspect the device cards, then select the named device. Addresses & interfaces and Static routes are two views of the same saved configuration.

guide.title: Configure and investigate
guide.why: Work from Client toward R1, R2 and the server, then trace the reply. More than one configuration fault is present.
guide.action: A correct Client /64, enabled R1 forwarding and a reachable R2 transit next hop solve different parts of the path.

guide.title: Verify the complete path
guide.why: A forward path alone is not enough. The simulated reply needs a working return route.
guide.action: Choose Check configuration. Open Inspect applied forwarding paths for the source, selected hops and reply; retry any failed requirement.

scenarios.explanation: The wrong Client prefix first sends remote traffic onto the local link. After correcting /64, R1 must forward to R2 through the transit-scoped neighbor. R2 can deliver to its branch interface and server, but the server still needs a route back through R2. Each repair has a distinct state effect; the final two-destination verification catches partial recovery.
hints: Work from Client toward R1, R2 and the server, then trace the reply. More than one configuration fault is present.
A correct Client /64, enabled R1 forwarding and a reachable R2 transit next hop solve different parts of the path.
If the branch router responds but the server fails, inspect the server’s return route. Forward delivery and a reply are separate results in the inspector.

requirements.label: Office reaches branch service and receives reply

ipv6_teaching.prerequisite_note: Capstone: combines the five preceding IPv6 lessons. Reopen their introductions if prefix, scope, route preference or forwarding is unfamiliar.

concepts.title: Investigate one failed segment at a time
concepts.text: Use the full task as a checklist: source prefix, selected next hop, transit forwarding and return route. Inspect applied paths after a check; a later failure can become visible only after an earlier fault is repaired.

concepts.title: Verify more than the gateway
concepts.text: Reaching a router’s own branch address does not prove the server has a reply route. Test both required destinations and keep the supplied address values. This capstone combines earlier concepts and native fields; no new command syntax is required.

ipv6_teaching.example_description: The practice branch has a wrong Client prefix, disabled R1 forwarding, a bad R1 transit next hop and no Server return route. Restore Client’s /64, enable R1 forwarding, route the branch through R2 at fe80::2 on transit, and give Server a default through fe80::1 on lan.

outcomes.label: Office reaches branch service and receives reply

ipv6_teaching.try_change: Remove only the Server default after the example passes. The branch router should still respond, while the server request arrives but its reply fails.
